title.title: Interoperability
title.subtitle: Why many chains need to talk — bridges, Cosmos IBC, Layer 0, and XRP

layer0Anim.headline: A tx travelling L2 → L1 → L0 → L1 → L2
steps: 1. L2 rollup posts a batch back to L1 (settlement)
2. L1 sends a cross-chain message through the Layer 0 hub
3. Layer 0 relays it to a different L1 (XCM / Warp / IBC)
4. Destination L1 delivers it down to its own L2

interop.heading: Why do blockchains need to talk to each other?
interop.subtitle: Every chain you have met so far keeps its own ledger, its own money and its own rules. None of them can read the others — by design.
interop.recap: Bitcoin (Section 01) · Ethereum (Section 02) · Hyperledger Fabric (Section 03) — each one is its own island
interop.analogy: Early email: a Gmail user could not write to a Hotmail user until providers agreed on a shared standard. Blockchains today are mostly still at the "no shared standard" stage.

svg.caption: Each island validates only its own ledger. A coin cannot "swim" across.

islands.title: Three problems that follow
islands.intro: They appear as soon as value or users want to move.

cards.title: Stranded assets
cards.desc: Bitcoin cannot be used inside an Ethereum app. To get it there, someone has to hold the real BTC and issue an IOU (WBTC) — so you now trust that someone.

cards.title: Fragile connections
cards.desc: Bridges, the connectors built so far, have lost more money than any other part of crypto.

cards.title: Split-up markets
cards.desc: Every chain has its own exchanges and pools. The same token can trade at different prices on different chains, and moving between them costs time and fees.

solutions.label: Layer 0
solutions.sub: One security team for many chains

usecases.heading: Where this shows up in real life
usecases.subtitle: Six everyday situations, and how value crosses today.

items.title: Moving to a cheaper lane
items.scenario: You hold ETH on Ethereum, but a swap costs $20 in fees. You move it to Arbitrum or Base, where the same swap costs cents.

items.title: Using Bitcoin in DeFi
items.scenario: You want to earn yield on BTC inside an Ethereum lending app. A custodian holds the BTC and issues WBTC you can use.

items.title: One stablecoin, many chains
items.scenario: USDC lives natively on a dozen-plus chains; Circle's CCTP burns it on one chain and mints it on another. RLUSD settles on XRPL and Ethereum.

items.title: Game items that travel
items.scenario: A game runs on its own chain for speed (Ronin, Immutable), but players want to sell items on an Ethereum marketplace.

items.title: Private data, public settlement
items.scenario: A consortium keeps supplier data on a private Fabric network but wants final settlement or tokens on a public chain for liquidity.

items.title: Cross-border payment routes
items.scenario: A payment starts as a stablecoin on one chain and must arrive as a local-currency token on another — in one trip, not three hops.

interopCompare.heading: Three ways to connect chains
interopCompare.subtitle: The question is the same each time: who do you trust for the hand-over?

col1.title: Bridges & Wrapped Tokens
col1.subtitle: Lock-and-mint · an operator in the middle
col1.analogy: A courier keeps your luggage and gives you a claim ticket to use in the other city.
col1.mechanism: Your coin is locked in a vault on chain A; a copy ("wrapped" token) is issued on chain B. Burn the copy to get the original back.
col1.trust: The bridge operators — usually a small group of signers who approve every release.
col1.risk: The vault holds everyone's coins in one place. If the signers' keys leak or the code has a bug, the whole vault goes.
col1.examples: WBTC · Ronin · Wormhole · Hop Protocol · LayerZero · Stargate

col2.title: Protocol-native / IBC
col2.subtitle: Chains verify each other directly
col2.analogy: Both airports read each other's boarding passes directly — no courier needed.
col2.mechanism: Each chain keeps a tiny copy of the other's block headers and checks the proof itself. Messages travel; coins are escrowed per connection, not in one giant vault.
col2.trust: The maths and the two chains' own validators — no extra company or committee.
col2.risk: Only as strong as the weaker of the two chains. Both must speak the same standard, which limits reach today.
col2.examples: Cosmos IBC (110+ chains) · IBC Eureka (Ethereum) · Polkadot XCM (within parachains)

col3.title: Layer 0 Network
col3.subtitle: One security team for many chains
col3.analogy: One security team guards every terminal in the airport — moving between terminals is just walking.
col3.mechanism: A shared validator set secures all connected chains at once, so sending a message between them is a built-in operation, not a separate contract.
col3.trust: The Layer 0's validators — the same people who finalise blocks also carry the messages.
col3.risk: Everything inside is as safe as the Layer 0 itself. To reach chains outside the club you still need a bridge.
col3.examples: Polkadot (Relay Chain + XCM) · Avalanche (Primary Network + Warp) · Babylon (BTC security layer)

layer0.heading: Layer 0 — shared security beneath the L1s
layer0.leadB: to many L1s at once, so a cross-chain call is a
layer0.inOneLine: Like an internet backbone: many ISPs (L1s) plug into shared cables (L0) instead of each laying their own.

provides.title: Shared security
provides.desc: A pooled validator set secures every L1 connected to it. New chains inherit security on day 1.

provides.title: Native cross-chain messaging
provides.desc: L0 defines the message format and trust model (XCM, Warp) — no third-party bridge needed.

provides.title: Shared infrastructure
provides.desc: Block production, finality, governance and upgrades live at L0. L1s focus on application logic.

layer02.heading: Layer 0: Known Platforms & Trade-offs
layer02.subtitle: Three Layer 0 networks, and how the model compares with Cosmos's sovereign chains.

platforms.tagline: Relay Chain + Parachains · XCM native messaging · Coretime model (2024)

bridges.heading: Bridges — useful, and the most hacked component in crypto
bridges.subB: was stolen from bridges in 2022 alone — about two-thirds of everything stolen in crypto that year.

vault.label: How a lock-and-mint bridge works
vault.caption: Every user adds to the same vault. The bigger it gets, the bigger the prize — that is the honeypot.

bridges.honest: Using a bridge is a trust decision, not a technical detail: you are trusting whoever controls the vault. Prefer a chain's official (canonical) bridge, and move only what you need.

hacks.name: Ronin Bridge
hacks.method: 5 of the 9 signer keys were stolen — enough to approve any withdrawal from the vault.

hacks.name: Wormhole Bridge
hacks.method: A signature check could be skipped — the attacker issued 120,000 wrapped ETH backed by nothing.

hacks.name: Nomad Bridge
hacks.method: A setup mistake made every message look valid. Hundreds of copycats emptied it within hours.

hacks.name: Harmony Horizon
hacks.method: Only 2 of 5 signers were needed — two stolen keys were enough.

dangers.title: One vault, everyone's coins
dangers.desc: The locked assets sit in a single contract. A bridge holding $500M is a $500M prize for whoever finds a bug.

dangers.title: A few people hold the keys
dangers.desc: Most bridges release funds when a small group of signers agree. Steal enough keys and the vault is yours.

dangers.title: Two chains, twice the complexity
dangers.desc: The bridge must understand both chains at once — different rules, timings and signature formats. More surface, more bugs.

safer.title: Chains verify each other (IBC)
safer.desc: No operator, no single vault — each chain checks the other's proofs. No known loss of funds from an IBC-protocol exploit so far.

safer.title: Official (canonical) bridges
safer.desc: Ethereum rollups' own bridges (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) are secured by the rollup's proof system, not by a separate group of signers.

safer.title: Rate limits & circuit breakers
safer.desc: Cap how much can leave per hour. Nomad was drained in minutes — a limit would have saved most of it.

wrapped.heading: What a wrapped token is
wrapped.subtitle: WBTC, wETH and friends are not the coin itself. They are a claim on a coin that someone else is holding.

svg.issuerPowers: can pause · can refuse to redeem
svg.caption: The wrapped balance is worth 1 BTC only while the custodian still holds 1 BTC and will hand it back.

cards.title: What it is
cards.desc: A token on one chain that stands for a coin held on another. 1 WBTC on Ethereum is a claim on 1 BTC kept by a custodian, much as a casino chip is a claim on cash at the cage.

cards.title: Who can redeem it
cards.desc: Usually not you. Only approved, identity-checked merchants swap WBTC back for BTC; everyone else sells it on an exchange. The price holds only while people believe the vault is full.

cards.title: Who can freeze it
cards.desc: The issuer. The WBTC contract can be paused by its owner, and a bridge operator can stop minting or releasing. If the vault is emptied, as at Wormhole in 2022, the copies are backed by nothing.

wrapped.noteLabel: Not every wrapper needs a custodian
wrapped.note: WETH on Ethereum itself is a plain contract: anyone swaps ETH for WETH and back 1:1 with nobody in the middle. The question to ask of any wrapped token is who holds the original.

bridgeHacks.heading: The four largest bridge hacks
bridgeHacks.subtitle: All in 2022, all on the same design: one vault, a few keys, one checking routine.

cosmos.heading: Cosmos: The Internet of Blockchains
cosmos.subtitle: Sovereign chains connected by the IBC protocol, each built for one use case.
cosmos.archNote: Zones can also IBC each other directly (mesh)

properties.title: IBC Protocol
properties.desc: Inter-Blockchain Communication: each chain verifies the other's block headers itself, so messages and assets move without a middleman.

properties.title: Cosmos SDK
properties.desc: Go framework with ready-made modules (staking, governance, IBC) for building an app-specific chain. Used by Osmosis, dYdX v4, Celestia and 100+ chains.

properties.title: CometBFT (ex-Tendermint)
properties.desc: The consensus engine, formerly Tendermint: ~1-second blocks, instant finality, no forks. Each zone has a known validator set and stays secure while fewer than one-third are dishonest.

properties.title: App-Specific Sovereignty
properties.desc: Each chain sets its own fees, governance and upgrades, and does not compete for block space with other apps.

cosmos.beyondBodyB: (live 2025) extends IBC to Ethereum and other non-Cosmos chains without a centralised bridge.
cosmos.dydx: dYdX, a derivatives exchange, left its Ethereum rollup in 2023 for its own Cosmos chain: an app gets its own chain once it is big enough to justify one.

xrp.heading: XRP Ledger — a purpose-built settlement rail

pillars.label: Native ops
pillars.title: DEX & payments are first-class
pillars.body: An order-book DEX has been built into the protocol since 2012; a native AMM (XLS-30) followed in 2024. The rule-set is fixed.

pillars.label: Federated validation
pillars.title: UNL — operators pick validators
pillars.body: Anyone can use the chain, but each node trusts a Unique Node List of validators; a round closes when 80% of them agree.

pillars.label: Cross-chain reach
pillars.title: One API to 50+ chains
pillars.body: Axelar lets XRPL apps send a payment and a message to EVM, Cosmos and other chains in one call, without a bridge contract per pair.

design.title: Fast & cheap by design
design.desc: 3–5 s finality and a few hundred tx/s in practice. Each transaction burns a tiny amount of XRP (~$0.0002), which deters spam; there is no fee market.

design.title: Trust Lines / IOUs
design.desc: Issued tokens (RLUSD, other stablecoins, tokenised assets) are balances on a Trust Line, a permission the holder grants the issuer.

design.title: Smart-contract logic lives off the base layer
design.desc: XRPL mainnet has no general smart contracts by design. Richer logic runs on side networks: the XRPL EVM sidechain (Solidity, 2025) and Xahau (Hooks).

design.title: Institutional use
design.desc: RLUSD, an NYDFS-regulated stablecoin (Dec 2024), settles on XRPL and Ethereum. Ripple's payment network uses XRP as a bridge currency, and CBDC pilots (Bhutan, Palau, Colombia) run on XRPL technology.

xrp.honestBody: A smaller smart-contract surface than the EVM, and federated validation: anyone can run a node, but the default validator list ships with the software. The bet is payments, tokenised assets and cross-chain settlement, not general-purpose apps.

quiz.question: Cross-chain bridges have been responsible for the largest hacks in crypto history — Ronin ($625M), Wormhole ($320M), Nomad ($190M). What architectural property makes bridges such high-value targets?
options: Bridges use proof-of-authority consensus controlled by a single company, making them easy to corrupt.
Bridges require KYC verification, creating a centralized identity database attackers can exploit.
Bridges concentrate large amounts of locked assets in a single smart contract on one chain while issuing representations on another — creating a honeypot with a single point of failure.
Bridges are slower than direct transactions, giving attackers more time to execute front-running attacks during the transfer window.
quiz.explanation: To bridge 1 ETH to another chain, you lock the ETH in a contract on Ethereum and mint a wrapped version on the destination. Every user's locked assets pile up in that one contract, so it becomes an ever more valuable target. Ronin held $625M before attackers compromised 5 of 9 validator keys and drained it. Bridges need a trusted group (validators or a multisig) to operate, which conflicts with blockchain's trust minimisation. IBC-style protocols avoid this by having chains verify each other directly.

takeaways.title: Section 04 — Key Takeaways
items: Each chain is an island: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Fabric cannot read each other's ledgers — so value and messages need a route
Real needs drive it: cheaper L2 lanes, Bitcoin in DeFi, stablecoins on many chains, game assets, private data with public settlement
Three routes, one question — who do you trust? Bridges: an operator. IBC: the maths and both chains. Layer 0: one shared validator set
Bridges are the most hacked component in crypto (Ronin $625M, Wormhole $320M); using one is a trust decision, so prefer official bridges
XRP Ledger is a payments rail that reaches other chains through Axelar rather than a bespoke bridge per pair

keyPoints.s4-interop: Every chain is an island by design; value only moves if someone builds a route and someone is trusted to run it.
keyPoints.s4-usecases: In every real case someone holds the asset or verifies the other chain; who that is, is the design question.
keyPoints.s4-interop-compare: Three routes, one question: do you trust an operator, the maths, or a shared validator set?
keyPoints.s4-chooser: The safest connection is the one with the fewest people to trust.
keyPoints.s4-bridges: Bridges are where most of the money has been stolen; using one is a trust decision.
keyPoints.s4-wrapped: A wrapped token is an IOU; it is worth the original only while someone holds that coin and agrees to give it back.
keyPoints.s4-bridge-hacks: Every big bridge hack came down to a few stolen keys or one bug in the vault's checks; one shared vault turned it into a total loss.
keyPoints.s4-cosmos: Cosmos trades shared security for sovereignty; IBC lets chains verify each other without a middleman.
keyPoints.s4-layer0: A Layer 0 is a security team for hire; new chains inherit protection on day one.
keyPoints.s4-layer0-2: Shared security or full sovereignty: you rent one or build the other.
keyPoints.s4-xrp: XRPL is a payments rail, not an app platform; it is fast and cheap because it does less.

scenarios.title: Move stablecoins to an L2
scenarios.desc: You hold USDC on Ethereum and want to use it on Arbitrum or Base, where fees are cents.

scenarios.title: One app, two chains, shared state
scenarios.desc: A lending app runs on two independent chains and needs balances and prices to stay in sync.

scenarios.title: Bank consortium meets a public chain
scenarios.desc: Banks run a private settlement chain but want tokens and final settlement on a public network.

bridge.label: Bridge
bridge.sub: Lock here, mint a copy there — an operator in the middle

ibc.label: IBC-style messaging
ibc.sub: Both chains verify each other's proofs directly

l0.label: Layer 0
l0.sub: Both chains sit under one shared validator set

bridge.text: Use the rollup's own (canonical) bridge. It is secured by the rollup's proof system, not by a separate group of signers.
bridge.risk: Going back to L1 is slow: hours on a ZK rollup, about 7 days on an optimistic one. 'Fast' third-party bridges fix that by adding an operator you must trust.

ibc.text: Ethereum and its rollups do not use IBC; the rollup already has a native, proof-secured route to L1.
ibc.risk: You would be building a second, less-tested path next to one that already exists.

l0.text: Arbitrum and Base are not parachains — there is no Layer 0 here. Ethereum itself is the shared security the rollups borrow.
l0.risk: Adding a Layer 0 means adding a validator set and a token you don't need for this job.

bridge.text: General message bridges (Axelar, LayerZero, Wormhole) can carry state updates between almost any two chains today — the widest reach.
bridge.risk: Your app's state now depends on the bridge's signer set. If it is compromised, both deployments can be corrupted at once — the honeypot problem.

ibc.text: If both chains speak IBC (Cosmos zones, or Ethereum via IBC Eureka), each verifies the other's proofs directly — messages travel without a middleman or a giant vault.
ibc.risk: Only as strong as the weaker chain, and both must implement the standard — reach is limited to the IBC ecosystem today.

l0.text: If both chains live inside the same Layer 0 (two parachains, two Avalanche L1s), messaging is native — XCM or Warp — and verified by the shared validators.
l0.risk: Only works inside the club. The moment one chain is outside, you are back to a bridge.

bridge.text: Anchor the private chain's state, or settle tokens, through a bridge the consortium controls. Simple and chain-agnostic — this is how most pilots start.
bridge.risk: The bridge operator is a single point of failure, and the regulator will ask who holds the keys. Governing that bridge becomes the real project.

ibc.text: A Fabric or Besu consortium chain does not speak IBC. You would have to rebuild it on an IBC-capable stack first — a migration, not an integration.
ibc.risk: A large rebuild for a standard the public chain you target may not support either.

l0.text: Run the consortium chain as a permissioned L1 inside a Layer 0 (an Avalanche L1 or a parachain). You keep your own validators and rules, yet messaging to the public network is native — the model JP Morgan piloted on Avalanche.
l0.risk: You are bound to that Layer 0's rules, token and validator security — and reaching chains outside it still needs a bridge.
